source_read: PDF, pp. 275–297 (all 23 pages read; Tables 1–3 and Figure 1 checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi)

claims.overstatement: Two qualifications from this source. (1) Publication bias: Scott et al. report no significant evidence of publication bias on visual inspection of a funnel plot (p. 284), so the claim's 'there is evidence of publication bias' rests on the later meta-analyses, not on this one. (2) Abstinence: in the 12 studies reporting it, mean abstinence was 295 days (SD 359, range 0–1241), and some samples were current users (p. 281). 'Mostly tested within their first months' fits this meta-analysis less well than the later ones. Minor: executive functions (−0.63) were as large as memory (−0.59), so 'largest for learning and memory' could read 'learning, executive function and memory'.
claims.note: Numbers checked. 17 studies, 471 users vs 445 comparison participants (p. 284), and Table 3 sums to 487/464 for 18 studies, minus Gonzalez et al. (16/19) = 471/445. Domain range −0.34 (language) to −0.66 (learning) (p. 284; Figure 1, p. 286). Sign: negative d = users worse (p. 282). Education: users 12.47 vs controls 13.87 years; 76% of studies not matched on education (pp. 284–285). This supports 'less education than controls in most studies'.

anchors.locator: Meta-analysis › Research Groups, last paragraph; Table 3 (p. 285)
anchors.extracted: One research group's study (d=−1.37) excluded, leaving 17 studies with 916 participants: 471 with methamphetamine abuse/dependence and 445 comparison participants (mean 53.9 per study, range 19–130). Before exclusion: 18 studies, 951 participants.

Domain means across 17 studies: learning −0.66, executive −0.63, memory −0.59, processing speed −0.52, motor −0.48, attention/working memory −0.39, visuoconstruction −0.37, language −0.34; all intervals exclude zero except simple reaction time (Figure 1: about −0.37, CI about −0.76 to 0.02). Domains differed (χ²=23.6, p<0.01).

Education: users 12.47 (SD 1.59; 15 studies, n=443) vs comparison 13.87 (SD 1.69; n=390). 76% of studies did not match groups on education; the education gap did not significantly moderate effect sizes (b=0.06, p=0.13).
Visual inspection of a funnel plot showed no significant evidence of publication bias; no formal test or trim-and-fill result reported.
Length of abstinence reported in 12 studies: mean 294.89 days (SD 359.37), range 0–1241; the review notes some included samples were current users abstinent only on the day of testing.

anchors.locator: Statistical Analyses, end of section; Figure 1 legend (p. 286)
anchors.extracted: Grand mean d=−0.558 (SE 0.034) with between-study variance 0.037 (p<0.01), computed on k=18 (including the later-excluded study); research groups differed significantly (χ²(10)=30.1, p<0.001; p. 284).

claims.note: Supports the cross-sectional part: abstinence length did not moderate effect sizes. The source does not say how many studies had samples abstinent more than a year; its study-level mean was about 10 months with a range up to 1241 days.

anchors.extracted: Neither average length of abstinence nor average duration of lifetime use had an appreciable influence on effect size (ps>0.10); prior non-methamphetamine substance disorders (excluded in 6 studies, not in 11) also made no significant difference.
Authors note the meta-analysis could not do finer analyses of abstinence or recovery and call for large longitudinal cohorts to test whether sustained abstinence brings full or partial recovery.
Abstinence data from only 12 of 17 studies; mean 294.89 days, SD 359.37, range 0–1241.

key_findings.correction: The 157 effect sizes were coded from all 18 studies (p. 282: range 1–19, mean 8.72 per study), not after the exclusion; the number remaining after excluding Gonzalez et al. (2007) is not reported. The same wording appears in the card's design_detail.
Also: more men and older age in the comparison group went with smaller differences (b=+0.01, p<0.01; b=+0.05, p=0.09) (p. 285).
The comparison uses the grand mean computed on 18 studies.

reporting_issues.note: Figure 1 legend '*k=18' (p. 286); grand mean on p. 283.
Volkow 2001b reported only non-significant within-user trends in 5 people with no control or normative comparison.
The 40% figure (p. 281) cannot be checked from this source; by its title in the reference list (p. 295), Rippeth et al. (2004) is a study of methamphetamine dependence and HIV infection.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low agreed. 'Duplicate study selection: yes' is generous: the two investigators searched independently, but independent eligibility decisions are not described (p. 282); partial-yes would be safer.

interpretation_gap.note: I would rate it moderate rather than minor. Beyond the frontostriatal attribution, the title and abstract frame the group differences as effects of methamphetamine. The Discussion states that the data support the notion that methamphetamine use disrupts memory encoding and retrieval (pp. 286–287), and the summary opens by calling methamphetamine neurotoxic (p. 290). These are causal readings of cross-sectional averages, although the review elsewhere concedes premorbid differences (pp. 288–289).

missed: Abstinence in the included samples averaged 295 days (SD 359, range 0–1241) across 12 studies, with current users included (pp. 281, 284). This bears on the encyclopedia's description 'mostly tested within their first months of abstinence' and could be a key finding.

Minor reporting inconsistency: the list of included studies in the acknowledgements gives Simon et al. 2000 and 2004 (p. 291), while Table 3 lists Simon et al. 2000 and 2002 (p. 285); relevant if overlap with later meta-analyses is assessed.
Minor: the Methods number the domains with a duplicated '(4)' and list nine domains (p. 282); the abstract says nine.
